The scope statement states specifically what business areas the project will include, what the project will produce, when it will be produced, and in some cases, how much the organization will pay for it. We recommend use of the ODW technique (Objectives, Deliverable and Workplan) to align the desired outcomes of the project with the project workplan.

Project scope must be clear and measurable. If the scope statement is unclear or difficult to measure, managing scope will be extremely difficult. Project scope cannot be adequately defined by a single dimension such as work or time; it must be defined from multiple perspectives. We recommend that 5 dimensions are considered to rigorously specify project scope. These are:

  1. Logical. Logical project scope is relevant only to model driven projects where the scope of activity is described in terms of a subset of the enterprise knowledge base.
  2. Deliverable. Deliverable scope refers to the deliverables and deliverable components that the project will produce. The deliverables are based on the project goals and should be the minimum set necessary to satisfy those goals.
  3. Financial. Financial scope is defined by the cost constraints on the project and its value to the enterprise.
  4. Temporal. Temporal scope refers to the project's start and end dates and any other external milestone dates that constrain it.
  5. Organizational. Organizational scope describes which organizational units will participate, either directly or indirectly, in the project.
Review project scope on a regular basis for updates and refinement.

Establishing project scope is perhaps the most critical part of planning a project. The project scope serves as the foundation for the entire project charter and informs the Statement of Work (SOW) for an engagement. The scope statement formally defines the work to be performed to deliver a capability, product, service, or result with the specified features and functions.
